claims.text: Tailored alloying and thermomechanical processing can enhance the distribution of alumina-forming elements in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Enhanced distribution of alumina-forming elements leads to a uniform, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale.
A uniform, adherent, and slow-growing oxide scale governs improved oxidation resistance and material integrity at high temperature.
Increasing and homogenizing additions of alumina-stabilizing elements, together with advanced thermomechanical processing, promotes favorable microstructural distributions.
The enhanced microstructure directs alumina-forming elements to segregate to the alloy surface.
Surface segregation of alumina-forming elements enables development of a continuous and adherent protective alumina or similar oxide scale.
A coherent, slow-growing oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
The protective scale minimizes oxygen ingress and retards degradation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will exhibit a lower oxidation rate as indicated by lower weight gain per unit area.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will form a more uniform and adherent surface oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline, the tailored alloy will retain better mechanical integrity after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The conventionally processed baseline alloy is expected to form a more discontinuous and rapidly growing oxide scale.
The discontinuous and rapidly growing baseline oxide scale is expected to cause accelerated degradation.
The proposed behavior requires sufficient concentrations of alumina-forming elements.
The hypothesis is expected to apply under continuous oxygen-rich oxidation at approximately 900–1200°C.
The proposed behavior may not hold outside approximately 900–1200°C or in atmospheres substantially different from the tested oxygen-rich atmosphere.
